prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept
Asset type: ONE seamless repeating GRASS GROUND TEXTURE TILE for a top-down Vietnamese Đông Hồ-inspired strategy game. Square 1024x1024 opaque image, artwork covers the entire canvas edge to edge.
The actual subject is the flat grass-covered land itself. A continuous pale sage-green grassy surface, with irregular low-contrast flat olive pigment areas and a few broad warm straw-colored exposed-earth passages weaving into the grass. Very small sparse grass blades represented by economical short hooked woodcut strokes across the ground. The grass forms one connected surface across all four edges.
Style: Vietnamese Đông Hồ folk woodblock printing translated into a quiet game terrain background. Flat restrained pigments, simplified hand-carved marks, subtle ink-registration irregularity, clean shapes. Ground marks are much lighter and smaller than the outlines on buildings and trees. The result must work underneath the game's existing ink-outlined trees, rice paddies, villages and mountains.
Palette: dominant pale sage #b7bf8d and muted olive #a7b47d, light straw #d9c692 earth, darker grass marks #89965f. Keep the overall value light and colors muted and warm so it fits parchment-colored game art. Broad flat color, very little contrast in large shapes, about 75% quiet space. Grass marks roughly 8–20 pixels tall, irregularly spaced; no large isolated tufts.
Tiling: opposite edges match seamlessly; texture continues beyond every edge, no border, no vignette, no spotlight, no central composition. This is a full-area surface tile, NOT a sheet of sprites or ornaments.
Exclude: decorative strips, isolated grass islands, leaf ornaments, raised mounds, paths with heavy outlines, any trees/buildings/mountains/objects/UI, transparent background, checkerboard, text, photographic microtexture, realistic lighting, shadows, 3D shading, glossy or pixel art. No subdivided grid or hex outlines.
packing: scripts/conquest-art/pack-grass-ground.mjs: resize to 512px and slice continuous world-coordinate samples into a shared atlas. No artistic repaint or per-cell randomization.
